Ankh Glycosylation Prediction — Interpretation Report

Source: Ankh_glycosylation_clean_pipeline.ipynb  |  Embeddings: Ankh-base • 768-dim  |  Task: binary protein-level glycosylation classification

1. Dataset

Proteins from the manually curated UniProt/Swiss-Prot human proteome were split into two mutually exclusive classes using the Glycosylation curated column:

  • Positive (glycosylated): column value is present (non-null)
  • Negative (not glycosylated): column value is missing (null)

Duplicate protein names were removed within each class and any overlap between classes was discarded, guaranteeing clean non-overlapping labels. This labelling procedure is identical to the ESM2 and ProtT5 pipelines, ensuring fair cross-model comparisons.

Figure 1. Class distribution. Glycosylated proteins represent 21.8% of the dataset.

Class imbalance note: With only 21.8% positive examples, PR-AUC (Average Precision) is the primary metric throughout. A random classifier would achieve PR-AUC ≈ 0.218. Models are trained with explicit imbalance corrections (balanced class weights for logistic regression; BCEWithLogitsLoss pos_weight = neg/pos for MLP).

2. Methods

2.1 Embeddings

Precomputed Ankh-base (Elnaggar et al., 2023) protein language model embeddings (768-dimensional) were loaded from a pre-built NPZ cache. Ankh is a T5-based protein language model trained on UniRef50/UniRef90. Two global sequence representations were evaluated:

  • Max pooling — element-wise maximum across the residue dimension
  • Attention pooling — learned weighted average across residues

All features were z-score normalised (StandardScaler) using training-set statistics only to prevent data leakage. Ankh’s 768-dim vectors are more compact than ESM2 (1280-dim) and ProtT5 (1024-dim).

2.2 Classifiers

All experiments use an 80/20 stratified train/test split (seed 42).

5. Interpretation and Discussion

5.1 Overall Performance

The best Ankh model (Mlp + ATTN pooling) achieves ROC-AUC = 0.9748 and PR-AUC = 0.9228. The PR-AUC of 0.9228 against a random baseline of 0.218 represents a 4.2× improvement over chance, confirming that Ankh’s 768-dim pooled embeddings encode detectable glycosylation signal at the protein level.

5.2 Ankh vs ESM2 / ProtT5 Comparison

Ankh produces more compact embeddings (768-dim) compared to ESM2 (1280-dim) and ProtT5 (1024-dim). Despite the lower dimensionality, Ankh embeddings often achieve competitive performance on downstream tasks because they are trained with a protein-optimised vocabulary and architecture. Direct numerical comparison with the ESM2 results (in results_glycosylation_ESM2/) and ProtT5 results (in results_glycosylation_ProtT5/) enables model selection for downstream applications.

5.3 Task-Specific Challenges

  • Class imbalance: Only 21.8% of proteins are labelled positive.
  • Label granularity: Glycosylation labels come from the curated UniProt Glycosylation column; this captures protein-level modification status but not specific glycosite positions.
  • Biological complexity: Glycosylation is heterogeneous; a global pooled vector cannot easily capture the localised sequence motifs that determine glycosylation susceptibility.
  • Information bottleneck: Pooling compresses all residue-level embeddings into one fixed-size vector, discarding positional context.

5.4 Pooling Strategy Comparison

Comparing the two pooling strategies for Ankh:

  • MLP: attention PR-AUC = 0.9228 vs max PR-AUC = 0.9214 (Δ = +0.0014)
  • Logistic Regression: attention PR-AUC = 0.9053 vs max PR-AUC = 0.8885 (Δ = +0.0168)

Attention pooling consistently outperforms max pooling, suggesting that the learned weighted residue aggregation in attention pooling better summarises glycosylation-relevant sequence features.

5.5 Model Architecture Comparison

The MLP’s capacity to model non-linear feature interactions provides a meaningful benefit over logistic regression for this task. The modest gain suggests that glycosylation signal in globally-pooled Ankh space is weakly non-linear.

5.6 Embedding Space Separability

PCA and t-SNE projections of Ankh attention embeddings show the degree of class separability in the high-dimensional representation space. Overlap between glycosylated (red) and non-glycosylated (blue) proteins in both projections reflects the difficulty of predicting glycosylation from a single global protein vector — residue-level per-token models targeting specific glycosylation motifs would be a natural next step.

5.7 Threshold Sensitivity

All confusion matrix values are at the default threshold of 0.5. The PR curves in Figure 3 provide a full operating range; lowering the threshold increases recall at the cost of more false positives and can be tuned per application.

6. Recommendations for Future Work

  1. Residue-level classifier: Train a per-token binary classifier on Ankh token embeddings to predict residue-level glycosylation likelihood directly.
  2. Structured labelling: Extract exact glycosite positions from the structured UniProt glycosylation annotations for cleaner, position-specific labels.
  3. Cross-validation: Replace the single 80/20 split with 5-fold stratified cross-validation for more robust metric estimates.
  4. Feature combination: Concatenate max-pool and attention-pool vectors (2×768-dim input) to capture complementary representations.
  5. Cross-model comparison: Directly compare Ankh results with ESM2 (results_glycosylation_ESM2/) and ProtT5 (results_glycosylation_ProtT5/) to identify the best backbone.
  6. Fine-tuning: Fine-tune Ankh end-to-end on the glycosylation task rather than using frozen embeddings.
